title: Weeds behind the palace
hookLine: courts are splendid while fields grow weeds; this is robbery (Tao Te Ching 53)
carry: splendor that starves the fields is theft

cards: The courtyard is swept so clean the stones shine. Silk at every shoulder. A polished sword at every hip.
Long tables, and more food than anyone can finish. Now walk out past the gate, past the last wall, to the fields that feed all of this. Thistles.

Nobody has worked them in a long time. And the storehouse meant for a lean winter is empty. Chapter fifty-three of the Tao Te Ching stands in that field, looks back at the shining courtyard, and gives it a blunt name.

teach.h: THE WAY IS EASY TO LEAVE.
teach.b: First, the speaker's worry. The chapter opens in the first person: if I had even a little knowledge, and walked the great way, the one thing I'd fear is straying from it.
Then a sigh: the great way is level and easy, and yet people love the side paths. The way isn't hard to find. It's easy to leave.
Second, the picture you just walked through.
The court is spotless, the fields are full of weeds, the granaries are empty. All three in one breath, so you can't look at one without the others. Third, the name.
Fine robes, sharp swords, too much food and drink, wealth piled past what anyone needs. The chapter calls this robbery, the swagger of a thief, and says flatly that it is not the Tao.
It doesn't call the court wicked for being clean.
In one reading, the pairing is the theft: shine in the courtyard, paid for by neglect in the field.
Fourth, the shape at home size. It comes in small sizes too.
A budget that polishes what visitors see while what's actually needed goes without. A life that looks great online while a sick friend hasn't had a call.
A company lobby with fresh flowers and a break room with a broken fridge. The question it leaves is plain: where are your fields, and what's growing in them?

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter fifty-three as a warning to anyone with means: splendor kept up while the fields and storehouses go neglected is, in the chapter's words, a kind of robbery.

games.q: what does “weeds in the fields” mean?
o: a shining court beside neglected, weedy fields
the poor farmers who stole from the court
a garden that needs more careful tending

p: fine robes and too much food

s: chapter fifty-three says the great way is hard to find
it says the way is level and easy, and yet people love the side paths.
the chapter names the splendid court beside weedy fields as robbery
it calls it the swagger of a thief, and says it is not the Tao.
the chapter opens in the first person
the speaker says that walking the great way, the one fear would be straying from it.

games.q: you rule a court that shines. past the gate, the fields are weedy and the granaries empty. what does chapter fifty-three say about your court?
o: it is robbery, and not the Tao.
it's fine, as long as the gate is guarded.
games.why: the chapter sets the spotless court beside the weeds and the empty granaries and names the whole display robbery, the swagger of a thief.

practice: Walk out past your own gate in your mind: a neighbor having a hard month, a coworker stretched thin, a cause you've meant to support.

Let one person or need come clearly to mind, and choose one concrete thing you could give: some money, a meal, an hour, a phone call. Hold that choice, something real and not grand, for the rest of the sit.
